title: Americans’ increased belief in voter fraud is a scary prospect in 2026 | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

President Donald Trumpmessing with the 2026 midtermsbeforehand — as he’s trying to do bysharply restricting mail ballots— is only part of the potential threat he’s posing to US elections.

The other is his demonstrated tendency for claiming elections have been stolen after the fact, which resulted in the largest attack on the US Capitol in 200 years.

New polling suggests Trump has kept that soil fertilized with a large portion of the country. Indeed, the president on Fridayposted on social mediathe 5-year-old video of him telling January 6, 2021, rioters to go home and repeating his false claim that he won in 2020.

And amid his repeated claims of widespread voter fraud, the polling suggests that soil might be even more fertile than its been in recent years, which is a scary prospect.

AQuinnipiac University pollshows a majority of registered voters (51%) are at least “somewhat concerned” that there will be widespread voter fraud in the upcoming election.

That’s actually 10 pointshigherthan the same question in a poll conductedjust before the 2022 midterm election.

The percentage today who say they are “very concerned” (29%) is also double-digits higher than it was four years ago (18%).

And the rise is overwhelmingly due to — no surprise — Republicans. The percentage who are at least “somewhat concerned” has risen from 59% to 74%, and the percentage who are “very concerned” has gone from 24% to 40%.

So even though 2022 was only a little removed from the fiasco after the 2020 election — in which large swaths of Trump’s base embraced his baseless claims of a stolen election, and some of them attacked the Capitol — concern about voter fraud is actually higher on the right today than it was back then.

(There has also been a small rise in concern among Democrats, but two-thirds of them say they are not that concerned.)

And this is not the only evidence that a large percentage of the electorate is primed to believe voter fraud could be a significant problem in 2026.

AnAP-NORC pollreleased last week showed the percentage of Americans who trusted government certifications of election results at least “quite a bit” dropping from 40% in 2024 to 34% today.

A March poll conducted for NPR and PBS byMarist Collegefound that 50% of Americans said voter fraud was likely in the 2026 elections. That’s similar to the 52% who said so inJanuary 2020, a year before the Capitol attack. (There was a slight drop in those who called it “very likely,” though.)

Republicans were also more likely to rank voter fraud as the biggest threat to American elections (57%) than they were six years ago (47%).

And aReuters-Ipsos pollin April showed a pretty substantial belief in what is arguably Trump’s biggest voter fraud hobbyhorse these days: the baselessclaim that many undocumented immigrants are votingin US elections.

The poll showed 46% of Americans, including 82% of Republicans, agreed that US elections include a “large number” of illegal votes by noncitizens.

And a 53% majority, including 83% of Republicans, were at least “somewhat concerned” about fraudulent mail-in or absentee ballots.

On both questions, only between 21% and 26% of Americans strongly embraced those positions. But there was another quarter of the population that was at least inclined toward them.

And that’s the danger here: a small but passionate group of people truly embraces the cause, just like they did after the 2020 election, while others who might not feel as strongly go along for the ride.

If there’s good news for our democracy, it’s that large numbers of Americans appear to be approaching Trump’s specific claims with at least a modicum of skepticism.

Afterhis July primetime addressfull of unproven claims about foreign election interference and a supposed coverup, Quinnipiac found that registered voterssaid 66%-24% that he had not provided sufficient evidenceto prove his claims.

Similarly, the AP poll this week showed 60% of Americans trust Trump to provide accurate information about the outcome of the 2026 election “only a little” (16%) or “not at all” (44%). Just 17% trust him at least “quite a bit.”

Indeed, the further away we got from the 2020 election, the more that even Trump’s election-denying supportersacknowledged there wasn’t actually solid evidencethat the election was stolen.

And if Trump remains even more unpopular than he was when he lost the 2020 campaign — as he is now — perhaps fewer people will be inclined to truly embrace his claims of another stolen election.

But despite Trump’s tortured history of barking up this tree, three new polls show half of Americans or more are at least a little on board with the concept of significant voter fraud in the 2026 election.

And the GOP writ large alsoquickly embraced baseless suggestions of fraudafter this year’s Los Angeles mayoral primary didn’t go their way.

It’s all rather inauspicious, given the recent history of elections that don’t go Trump’s way. And it’s worth paying attention to.
